simplifiedPassage.title: The Pirates of the Ancient Mediterranean (Simplified)

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Many people imagine pirates as wild adventurers on ships in the Caribbean Sea. But pirates were active in the Mediterranean much earlier than that, from the first millennium BCE. They attacked merchant ships and threatened important trade routes. Ancient states tried hard to stop them, but they could not. Piracy stayed a big problem for thousands of years. Only when pirates began to threaten Rome directly did Rome take action. The Roman general Pompey organised a large fleet, and Rome finally ended piracy in the Mediterranean.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Piracy in the Mediterranean was first written down in ancient Egypt, during the time of Pharaoh Amenhotep III. However, piracy probably started even earlier. The Mediterranean region was important, but some areas were rugged and mountainous. People who lived there depended on the sea for food and other resources, so they had boats and strong sailing skills. Because of this, it was easy for them to become pirates. The coastline also had many small coves, so pirates could hide their boats there. Before the 15th century, ships could not travel easily across open water. Because of this, ships had to follow a few well-known routes close to the coast, and this made slow merchant ships an easy target for pirates.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Sometimes, governments used pirates to help them, especially during wars. Pirates would attack first, before the government's own navy arrived. Because of this, some regions became rich by giving pirates a safe place to stay.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The first written record of a named pirate group was found in the Amarna Letters. These letters were messages between the Egyptian pharaoh and other rulers. Although the Egyptian fleet tried hard to stop the pirates, the pirates still caused a lot of trouble for trade. In one letter, the king of Alashiya said his people were not connected to the pirates, and he promised to punish anyone from his country who was involved in piracy.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The ancient Greeks had a different attitude towards piracy than the Egyptians did. Because the Greeks depended on the sea for almost everything, they saw pirates differently. In fact, famous Greek writers like Homer often praised pirates in their stories. Some important Greek officials even took part in piracy themselves. For example, in 355 BCE, some Athenian ambassadors stopped their official journey to capture a ship and take goods from it for themselves. Although the Greeks did not always accept piracy, there were too many pirates for the government to stop.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: As Rome became more powerful, it had to deal with piracy too. Piracy caused problems for Rome, but it also brought benefits, so Rome did not always fight against it. For example, pirates provided slaves for Roman farms and mines. However, when pirates attacked ships carrying grain to Rome, people in the Senate became angry and demanded punishment. Rome did not act quickly, so piracy continued. By the 1st century BCE, pirates became bold enough to kidnap important Roman officials and demand a ransom. The most famous hostage was Julius Caesar, who was captured in 75 BCE.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: By this time, Rome understood that piracy could not continue. In 67 BCE, a new law gave Pompey control of a large fleet. He divided the Mediterranean into 13 areas, and each area had its own commander. His forces cleared the pirates from one area before moving to the next. Eventually, the whole Mediterranean was free of pirates. Although thousands of pirates were killed, many others were given farmland far from the sea. In this way, Rome turned a dangerous problem into a benefit for its economy.

originalPassage.title: The pirates of the ancient Mediterranean
originalPassage.author: In the first and second millennia BCE, pirates sailed around the Mediterranean, attacking ships and avoiding pursuers

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: When one mentions pirates, an image springs to most people's minds of a crew of misfits, daredevils and adventurers in command of a tall sailing ship in the Caribbean Sea. Yet from the first to the third millennium BCE, thousands of years before these swashbucklers began spreading fear across the Caribbean, pirates prowled the Mediterranean, raiding merchant ships and threatening vital trade routes. However, despite all efforts and the might of various ancient states, piracy could not be stopped. The situation remained unchanged for thousands of years. Only when the pirates directly threatened the interests of ancient Rome did the Roman Republic organise a massive fleet to eliminate piracy. Under the command of the Roman general Pompey, Rome eradicated piracy, transforming the Mediterranean into 'Mare Nostrum' (Our Sea).

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Although piracy in the Mediterranean is first recorded in ancient Egypt during the reign of Pharaoh Amenhotep III (c 1390-1353 BCE), it is reasonable to assume it predated this powerful civilisation. This is partly due to the great importance the Mediterranean held at this time, and partly due to its geography. While the Mediterranean region is predominantly fertile, some parts are rugged and hilly, even mountainous. In the ancient times, the inhabitants of these areas relied heavily on marine resources, including fish and salt. Most had their own boats, possessed good seafaring skills, and unsurpassed knowledge of the local coastline and sailing routes. Thus, it is not surprising that during hardships, these men turned to piracy. Geography itself further benefited the pirates, with the numerous coves along the coast providing places for them to hide their boats and strike undetected. Before the invention of ocean-going caravels in the 15th century, ships could not easily cross long distances over open water. Thus, in the ancient world most ships were restricted to a few well-known navigable routes that followed the coastline. Caught in a trap, a slow merchant ship laden with goods had no other option but to surrender. In addition, knowledge of the local area helped the pirates to avoid retaliation once a state fleet arrived.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: One should also add that it was not unknown in the first and second millennia BCE for governments to resort to pirates' services, especially during wartime, employing their skills and numbers against their opponents. A pirate fleet would serve in the first wave of attack, preparing the way for the navy. Some of the regions were known for providing safe harbours to pirates, who, in return, boosted the local economy.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: The first known record of a named group of Mediterranean pirates, made during the rule of ancient Egyptian Pharaoh Akhenaten (c 1353-1336 BCE), was in the Amarna Letters. These were extracts of diplomatic correspondence between the pharaoh and his allies, and covered many pressing issues, including piracy. It seems the pharaoh was troubled by two distinct pirate groups, the Lukka and the Sherden. Despite the Egyptian fleet's best efforts, the pirates continued to cause substantial disruption to regional commerce. In the letters, the king of Alashiya (modern Cyprus) rejected Akhenaten's claims of a connection with the Lukka (based in modern-day Turkey). The king assured Akhenaten he was prepared to punish any of his subjects involved in piracy.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The ancient Greek world's experience of piracy was different from that of Egyptian rulers. While Egypt's power was land-based, the ancient Greeks relied on the Mediterranean in almost all aspects of life, from trade to warfare. Interestingly, in his works the Iliad and the Odyssey, the ancient Greek writer Homer not only condones, but praises the lifestyle and actions of pirates. The opinion remained unchanged in the following centuries. The ancient Greek historian Thucydides, for instance, glorified pirates' daring attacks on ships or even cities. For Greeks, piracy was a part of everyday life. Even high-ranking members of the state were not beyond engaging in such activities. According to the Greek orator Demosthenes, in 355 BCE, Athenian ambassadors made a detour from their official travel to capture a ship sailing from Egypt, taking the wealth found onboard for themselves! The Greeks' liberal approach towards piracy does not mean they always tolerated it, but attempts to curtail piracy were hampered by the large number of pirates operating in the Mediterranean.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: The rising power of ancient Rome required the Roman Republic to deal with piracy in the Mediterranean. While piracy was a serious issue for the Republic, Rome profited greatly from its existence. Pirate raids provided a steady source of slaves, essential for Rome's agriculture and mining industries. But this arrangement could work only while the pirates left Roman interests alone. Pirate attacks on grain ships, which were essential to Roman citizens, led to angry voices in the Senate, demanding punishment of the culprits. Rome, however, did nothing, further encouraging piracy. By the 1st century BCE, emboldened pirates kidnapped prominent Roman dignitaries, asking for a large ransom to be paid. Their most famous hostage was none other than Julius Caesar, captured in 75 BCE.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: By now, Rome was well aware that pirates had outlived their usefulness. The time had come for concerted action. In 67 BCE, a new law granted vast funds to Pompey to combat the Mediterranean menace. Taking personal command, Pompey divided the entire Mediterranean into 13 districts, assigning a fleet and commander to each. After cleansing one district of pirates, the fleet would join another in the next district. The process continued until the entire Mediterranean was free of pirates. Although thousands of pirates died at the hands of Pompey's troops, as a long-term solution to the problem, many more were offered land in fertile areas located far from the sea. Instead of a maritime menace, Rome got productive farmers that further boosted its economy.

grammarTools.title: Grammar Tool 1: Concession clauses (although / despite)
grammarTools.staticIntroHTML:
Step 1: Look at the passage

Bước 1: Nhìn vào bài đọc

“Despite the Egyptian fleet's best efforts, the pirates continued to cause substantial disruption to regional commerce.”

Dù hạm đội Ai Cập đã cố gắng hết sức, cướp biển vẫn tiếp tục gây xáo trộn lớn cho thương mại khu vực.

“Although piracy was a serious issue for the Republic, Rome profited greatly from its existence.”

Mặc dù cướp biển là vấn đề nghiêm trọng với nền Cộng hòa, La Mã vẫn hưởng lợi lớn từ sự tồn tại của nó.

Step 2: Notice

Bước 2: Nhận xét

What does 'although / despite' tell the reader? → the second part of the sentence is surprising, or opposite to what we would expect.

'Although / despite' cho người đọc biết điều gì? → vế sau của câu là điều bất ngờ, hoặc trái ngược với điều ta mong đợi.

patternExercise.title: Step 3: Discover the pattern
patternExercise.instructions: Complete the sentence. / Điền vào chỗ trống.

items.sentenceHTML: After although / despite, we usually expect one result — but the rest of the sentence gives a {{blank}} (surprising / opposite) result.

grammarTools.staticReadingToolHTML:
Step 4: Use it as a READING TOOL

Bước 4: Dùng làm công cụ đọc hiểu

When you see 'although' or 'despite', expect two opposite ideas. The MAIN message is usually the part after the comma.

Khi thấy 'although' hoặc 'despite', hãy chờ đợi 2 ý trái ngược nhau. Ý CHÍNH thường nằm ở phần sau dấu phẩy.

Example: “Although piracy was a serious issue for the Republic, Rome profited greatly from its existence.”

Ví dụ: 'Mặc dù cướp biển là vấn đề nghiêm trọng với nền Cộng hòa, La Mã vẫn hưởng lợi lớn từ sự tồn tại của nó.'

Core meaning: Rome profited from piracy.

Ý cốt lõi: La Mã đã hưởng lợi từ nạn cướp biển.

grammarTools.title: Grammar Tool 2: Participle clauses
grammarTools.staticIntroHTML:
Step 1: Look at the passage

Bước 1: Nhìn vào bài đọc

“Caught in a trap, a slow merchant ship had no other option but to surrender.”

Bị mắc bẫy, con tàu buôn chậm chạp không còn lựa chọn nào khác ngoài đầu hàng.

“Taking personal command, Pompey divided the entire Mediterranean into 13 districts.”

Tự mình chỉ huy, Pompey chia toàn bộ Địa Trung Hải thành 13 khu vực.

“Emboldened pirates kidnapped prominent Roman dignitaries.”

Được tiếp thêm sự táo bạo, cướp biển đã bắt cóc các quan chức La Mã cấp cao.

Step 2: Notice

Bước 2: Nhận xét

Who/what is 'caught in a trap'? → the merchant ship (something HAPPENED TO it). Who 'took personal command'? → Pompey (HE performed the action).

Ai/cái gì 'bị mắc bẫy'? → con tàu buôn (một việc XẢY RA VỚI nó). Ai 'tự mình chỉ huy'? → Pompey (CHÍNH ÔNG thực hiện hành động).

patternExercise.title: Step 3: Discover the pattern
patternExercise.instructions: Complete the sentence. / Điền vào chỗ trống.

items.sentenceHTML: A participle clause is a shortened way of writing a clause with because/when/as. It does not have its own {{blank}} — it shares the subject of the main clause.

grammarTools.staticReadingToolHTML:
Step 4: Use it as a READING TOOL

Bước 4: Dùng làm công cụ đọc hiểu

Expand the participle clause into a full clause to understand the meaning clearly.

Mở rộng mệnh đề rút gọn thành mệnh đề đầy đủ để hiểu rõ nghĩa.

Example: “Caught in a trap, a slow merchant ship had no other option but to surrender.”

Ví dụ: 'Bị mắc bẫy, con tàu buôn chậm chạp không còn lựa chọn nào khác ngoài đầu hàng.'

Expanded: Because the merchant ship was caught in a trap, it had no other option but to surrender.

Mở rộng: Vì con tàu buôn bị mắc bẫy, nó không còn lựa chọn nào khác ngoài đầu hàng.

grammarTools.staticReturnHTML:
Step 5: Return to the IELTS task

Bước 5: Quay lại vận dụng vào đề

Passage idea: “Taking personal command, Pompey divided the entire Mediterranean into 13 districts, assigning a fleet and commander to each.”

Ý trong bài: 'Tự mình chỉ huy, Pompey chia toàn bộ Địa Trung Hải thành 13 khu vực, mỗi khu vực có 1 hạm đội và 1 chỉ huy riêng.'

This sentence explains exactly HOW Pompey carried out his campaign — useful for a question about 'details of how a campaign to eradicate piracy was carried out'.

Câu này giải thích chính xác Pompey đã thực hiện chiến dịch NHƯ THẾ NÀO — hữu ích cho câu hỏi về 'chi tiết cách chiến dịch xóa sổ cướp biển được thực hiện'.
